Each item gives a high-resolution screenshot of professional software, across 23 applications in five industries and three operating systems, plus a written instruction, and the model must point to the matching element. A prediction counts as correct if its predicted point falls inside the target element's bounding box.

about.maintainer: Hwiwon Lee, Jiawei Liu, Dongjun Kim, Wubing Xia, Ziqi Zhang, Chunqiu Steven Xia and Lingming Zhang
about.notes: Maintainer detail: authors; affiliations not shown on the arXiv page. Printed label says OpenAI, which is not the paper's maintainer; the authors are academic. The GPT-6 Astra system card lists SEC-Bench Pro among OpenAI's cyber evaluations. Aggregator leaderboards disagree on the top score, so no score is given. The paper is a follow-up to the earlier SEC-bench (NeurIPS 2025). v1 was posted 2026-05-26 and v2 revised 2026-07-20.
about.what_it_tests: SEC-bench Pro tests whether AI coding agents can find real, previously disclosed security bugs in large, critical software, mainly the V8 and SpiderMonkey JavaScript engines. It contains 183 validated cases, each packaged in a container with a fixed version and a checkable crash result. The agents work without hints such as sanitizer output that names the vulnerable function, and the authors use an LLM judge to grade results.

about.maintainer: Academic author team led by Xiangyi Li
about.notes: Maintainer detail: with Wenbo Chen, Yimin Liu, Shenghan Zheng, Han-chung Lee and others (about 42 authors; affiliations not confirmed. Posted to arXiv 2026-02-13; built on the Harbor framework. Printed label says Alibaba, which no source confirms. Arcade.dev's 'SkillBench' is a different project (a scoring index of skills) and is not this benchmark.
about.what_it_tests: SkillsBench tests whether reusable instruction packages, called skills, actually help AI agents on real tasks. It has about 84 to 86 tasks across 11 domains (sources differ on the count), each with an automatic checker that decides pass or fail. Each task is run with no skills, with curated skills, and with skills the model wrote itself; curated skills raised average pass rates by about 16 percentage points, while self-written skills gave no average gain.

about.maintainer: Vals AI publishes and hosts the benchmark page
about.notes: Maintainer detail: DAPLab at Columbia University lists it as its project; paper authors Jeremy Spence, Nicholas Assaderaghi, Jinhao Zhu, Nikil Ravi and others. Printed label says OpenAI, and the name is misleading: 'SRE' here does not mean site reliability engineering. The Vals AI page and the DAPLab page both claim it, and the paper (arXiv 2608.11469, first posted 2026-08-11, revised 2026-10-01) lists its authors without a single institution, so the maintainer is given as both. The DAPLab page marks it 'In progress'. The GPT-6 Astra system card lists SRE-Bench as an OpenAI evaluation with pass@1 and pass@4 scores; the card's figures are not quoted here.
about.what_it_tests: SRE-Bench is a reverse-engineering benchmark, not a site-reliability one: it tests whether AI agents can work out what a compiled program does when no source code is given. Agents use a shell sandbox with standard analysis tools across five areas (network protocols, firmware, games, file-format recovery and malware). The benchmark has 262 binaries and 1,572 tasks that are graded deterministically.

about.notes: Scale Labs published it on September 19, 2025. The original launch figures (top models below 25 percent) reflect 2025 models and are far below current third-party leaderboard figures. The paper's authors are listed under Scale Labs. The 'printed by Google, Alibaba' labels were not checked against model cards.
about.what_it_tests: SWE-Bench Pro tests AI agents on realistic, long-horizon software engineering tasks in real codebases, often requiring multi-file patches that a professional engineer might take hours or days to finish. It has 1,865 problems from 41 actively maintained repositories, split into a public set, a held-out set and a commercial set from startup partners. Results are reported as Pass@1 under a unified scaffold, and a patch counts only if it passes the verifying tests.

about.notes: Maintainer detail: (first author Rishi Desai; affiliations not shown on the NeurIPS page); the xAI attribution rests on a third-party review of Grok 4.5 launch numbers. The xAI 29.0 percent pass@1 figure for Grok 4.5 comes from a third-party review page, not an xAI primary source, and was not verified. An AI Engineer talk reported a historical best of 26 percent. The paper reports that about 18.8 percent of rollouts showed reward hacking. The NeurIPS 2026 poster page gives no author affiliations, so the xAI link is unconfirmed.
about.what_it_tests: SWE-Marathon tests whether AI agents can autonomously complete ultra-long software work. It has 20 long-horizon tasks across software engineering and adjacent technical fields, each with a unique executable environment, a human-written reference solution and a multi-layer verification suite. A task counts as resolved when the verifier accepts the agent's work, and the paper says frontier coding agents resolve fewer than 20 percent of tasks.

about.notes: Maintainer detail: run through the Harbor framework. Project leads named in the repository README: Ryan Marten, Alex Shaw, Andy Konwinski, Ludwig Schmidt. Maintainers and sandboxed-container design come from the GitHub README. The May 19, 2025 launch date comes from a tbench.ai page seen only in search snippets. The Version 2.0 facts (89 tasks, November 7, 2025) come from secondary coverage. The README does not describe scoring; the leaderboard is on Harbor Hub.
about.what_it_tests: Terminal-Bench tests whether an AI agent can finish real jobs by typing commands into a Linux terminal, such as building software, configuring a system or processing files. Each task runs in its own sandboxed container, and the agent succeeds only if the final state of that container passes the task's automatic checks. Version 2.0 (November 2025) has 89 hand-checked tasks, and the companion Harbor framework runs the agents.

about.maintainer: Terminal-Bench-Science team, led by researchers at Stanford University, built with the Terminal-Bench and Harbor team
about.notes: The citation dates v0.1.0 to August 2026 and the page gives no exact release date. The page does not report a cost-per-task metric; it reports total cost across the 70 tasks, so the catalog's average-cost label is not supported. Top-model results conflict between tbench.ai (30%) and Snorkel pages (40%), so no score is given.
about.what_it_tests: Terminal-Bench-Science tests AI agents on the computational workflows working scientists actually run, not textbook questions. Each task is a containerised terminal job, such as statistical analysis, simulation, signal processing or proofs, and the output is checked by task-specific automated tests. Version 0.1 has 70 tasks written by practising researchers across life, physical, Earth, mathematical and engineering sciences.

about.notes: Maintainer detail: (Junlong Li, Junxian He and co-authors), with collaborators at All Hands AI, Carnegie Mellon and Duke. Accepted to ICLR 2026; code at github.com/hkust-nlp/toolathlon. The paper's first version names a different top model than a later version, so leaderboard leaders depend on the version cited. Printed label says Alibaba, which no source confirms. The 'Verified (Pass@1)' label refers to a subset or setting that was not checked in this run.
about.what_it_tests: Toolathlon (The Tool Decathlon) tests whether language agents can finish long, realistic workflows across many software applications. It covers 32 applications and 604 tools, from calendars and notes to databases and cloud consoles, with 108 tasks that take about 20 turns on average. Each task has its own automatic check of the final state, and the environments run in isolated containers.

about.notes: The Vals page gives version history from v1 to v2.1 (v2 on August 13, 2026; v2.1 on September 25, 2026) but not the original introduction date. Third-party mirrors (BenchLM, capitalandcompute) show earlier versions with different scores and leaders, which are not comparable.
about.what_it_tests: The Vals Index is a single composite score from Vals AI that averages agentic tasks in finance, coding, legal and tax work. Each sector is weighted by its share of US GDP, with finance carrying the most weight, and each sector score is the average of its benchmarks. The current version, 2.1, combines Finance Agent v2 and an Excel modeling benchmark for finance, Terminal-Bench 4.0, Vibe Code Bench and a code migration task for coding, and legal and tax benchmarks.

about.notes: Maintainer detail: with paper authors Hung Tran, Langston Nashold, Rayan Krishnan, Antoine Bigeard and Alex Gu. Paper submitted March 4, 2026 (v3 May 13, 2026), accepted to ACM CAIS 2026. The best test-split result of 61.8% was reported in the paper; leaderboard figures for later v1.1 and 1-100 variants come from aggregators and are not repeated here. A search snippet linked MIT researchers to the paper, which the arXiv page did not confirm.
about.what_it_tests: Vibe Code Bench tests whether an AI model can build a complete, working web application from a written description, starting from nothing. The benchmark has 100 app specifications split into validation and held-out test sets. An automated browser agent then checks each deployed app against 964 multi-step user workflows, and the score is the accuracy across their 10,131 steps.

about.notes: Maintainer detail: with the Center for AI Safety; lead authors include Jasper Gotting and Pedro Medeiros, with Seth Donoughe as corresponding author. A SecureBio newsletter describes a 350-question version, which differs from the 322 in the paper; the arXiv v2 is used here. Model scores come from a 2025 paper and are dated.
about.what_it_tests: The Virology Capabilities Test is a set of 322 multimodal questions, written with dozens of PhD-level virologists, about troubleshooting complex virology lab protocols. The questions cover factual, tacit and image-based knowledge, and models are scored by accuracy. In the April 2025 paper, expert virologists averaged about 22 percent on questions in their own sub-areas, and the best model listed there scored about 44 percent.

about.notes: Maintainer detail: co-first and corresponding authors listed on the arXiv paper. arXiv 2508.07999 (August 2025). Project page widesearch-seed.github.io; dataset and code are on Hugging Face and GitHub under ByteDance-Seed. Printed label says Alibaba, which no source confirms.
about.what_it_tests: WideSearch tests whether AI search agents can gather a large amount of information completely and accurately, such as a full table of facts about many entities, rather than a single answer. It has 200 questions in English and Chinese across more than 15 domains, drawn from real user queries, and each asks for many facts that are checked one at a time. The main score is an exact match to the reference table, and most systems scored close to zero while the best scored about 5 percent.

about.notes: Maintainer detail: with Scale AI and a group of academic and technical partners; authors include Nathaniel Li, Alexander Pan and Dan Hendrycks. The number of questions differs by version: the early paper and CAIS blog cite 4,157, and later versions and the GitHub README cite 3,668. The WMDP-Bio, WMDP-Chem and WMDP-Cyber labels are the three subsets.
about.what_it_tests: WMDP is a set of multiple-choice questions that serve as a proxy for hazardous knowledge in biosecurity, cybersecurity and chemical security. The questions were filtered by experts to remove sensitive and export-controlled details. Models are scored by accuracy, and the same questions are used in unlearning research, where the aim is to lower accuracy on the hazard questions while keeping general ability.

about.notes: The only candidate is an individual's Substack post found by search. It is not confirmed to be the benchmark Alibaba printed; the Qwen3.8 page lists WorkSpaceBench only as a row in its General Agent results table. The family may need to be dropped or re-scoped. Both WebFetch and the workstation browser were blocked on the post.
about.what_it_tests: WorkspaceBench is described in one post as a benchmark for agents working in OpenBB Workspace, where the durable state of the workspace is graded, for example whether a widget is in the correct dashboard and tab. The post could not be opened in this run because the site's bot check blocked the fetch, so the task count, inputs and scoring are not known. The Alibaba table row that prints the name has no description, method or citation.

about.notes: Written from xAI's own Grok 4.7 model card, read with pdftotext. FORTRESS is a Scale AI benchmark (Knight, Deshpande et al., 2025, arXiv 2506.14922, cited in the card's reference list); the FORTRESS-RN variant is named in the card and its link to the public suite is not further documented there. The card gives no release year, so introduced is null. The printed label reads CBRN / weapons refusals, which matches the card heading.
about.what_it_tests: xAI's Grok 4.7 model card (section 9.3, CBRN / weapons refusals) reports how often the model refuses requests about chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear weapons. The bio and chem parts use xAI's internal Autointent-Bio and Autointent-Chem suites of dangerous and benign CBRN queries, and the radiological and nuclear part uses FORTRESS-RN, a variant of the FORTRESS family of safeguard tests. The results are reported as refusal recall and refusal accuracy figures, and the card does not state the number of queries.

about.notes: Written from xAI's own Grok 4.7 model card, read with pdftotext. The card gives no release year, so introduced is null. Test content is described only at the level the card gives.
about.what_it_tests: xAI's Grok 4.7 model card (section 9.2, Child safety) describes an internal multi-turn evaluation of whether the model withholds assistance on child sexual exploitation, including CSAM. The prompts sit in the highest-severity child-safety category and unfold over a scripted conversation rather than a single message. A grader model judges each response against policy, and the reported figure is compliance, the share of dialogues that fail that judgment, where lower is better. The card does not state the number of dialogues.

about.notes: Written from xAI's own Grok 4.7 model card, read with pdftotext. The card does not state the number of items or a release year, so those are null or omitted.
about.what_it_tests: xAI's Grok 4.7 model card (section 9.1, General refusals) describes an internal evaluation of policy-following on harmful requests. The prompts span the major disallowed categories, from overt asks to well-hidden intent, and are written in English, Spanish, Chinese, Japanese, Arabic and Russian. A grader model judges each response against policy, and the reported figure is compliance, the share of items that fail that judgment, where lower is better.

about.notes: Written from xAI's own Grok 4.7 model card, read with pdftotext. The card names StrongREJECT but gives no reference for it, so that suite's authors are not stated here. The card does not state a release year or the number of attacks.
about.what_it_tests: xAI's Grok 4.7 model card (section 8.1, Jailbreaks) reports how often the model complies with attacks that should be refused. It has three parts: a battery of standard jailbreaks, both published and internally discovered; StrongReject, the StrongREJECT suite; and long-horizon multi-turn jailbreaks, including Crescendo attacks. Each part is reported as compliance, the share of should-refuse attacks answered with disallowed help, and lower is better.

about.notes: Written from xAI's own Grok 4.7 model card, read with pdftotext. The card gives no release year or prompt count.
about.what_it_tests: xAI's Grok 4.7 model card (section 10.1, Self-harm refusals, in its mental-health part) checks whether the model declines to help with requests related to self-harm, including longer conversations, while still offering support and resources. A response also fails if the model refuses without redirecting the user to help, or cannot recognise the intent behind a message that implies self-harm or crisis. The reported figure is compliance, where a lower score is better, and the card does not describe the prompts.

about.notes: Written from xAI's own Grok 4.7 model card, read with pdftotext. The card gives no release year or item count. The card files it under its Behaviors part, section 11.
about.what_it_tests: xAI's Grok 4.7 model card (section 11.2, Sycophancy) describes an internal evaluation of whether the model abandons a correct answer when a user confidently states a wrong one. The items are factual questions in science, history and other general-knowledge topics, each paired with misleading user-supplied context. A grader compares the answer with the true answer, and the sycophancy rate is the share of items where the model follows the user instead of the correct answer, where lower is better.

about.notes: The arXiv abstract (submitted 13 February 2025, revised 7 July 2026; ICML 2026) gives the purpose, the metrics and the release and one-year results. The question counts and the Cambridge affiliation come from the paper body as reported in secondary coverage, not from the abstract. "ZeroBench-main" on a model card is the 100 main questions.
about.what_it_tests: ZeroBench tests visual reasoning in multimodal models with questions filtered to be impossible for frontier models when it was built: 100 curated main questions plus 334 subquestions that break them into steps. The metrics are pass@1, pass^5 (all five attempts correct) and pass@5 (any of five attempts correct). At release every tested model scored 0% on pass@1 and pass^5; a year later the state of the art reached 6% pass^5 and 19% pass@5.
